what_it_does: This paper designs a low-power circuit for automotive touch-screen sensors that detects when you touch the screen while meeting strict electromagnetic interference (EMI) regulations. The problem is that the sensors typically operate at high frequencies (200–500 kHz) to drive the touch surface, and these high-frequency signals radiate radio-frequency noise that violates automotive EMI standards. The team's solution is to reshape the driving signal using two techniques: pipelined dual-frequency modulation (switching between two frequencies in a controlled pattern) and sine-squared waveform shaping (smoothing out the sharp edges of the signal). These tricks scatter the radio-frequency energy across a broader spectrum where it doesn't violate emissions limits, while keeping the sensor sensitive and responsive.
